questions.question: What is the difference between DDL, DML, and DQL in SQL?
questions.title: DDL vs DML vs DQL in SQL
questions.direct_answer: SQL commands can be grouped by purpose. **DDL** defines database objects, with commands such as `CREATE`, `ALTER`, and `DROP`. **DML** changes rows with `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, and `DELETE`. **DQL** is a common teaching name for reading data with `SELECT`. These labels do not decide whether a statement auto-commits; transaction behaviour depends on the database.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can separate schema changes, row changes, and queries without turning a database-specific transaction rule into a universal SQL rule.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying that DDL always auto-commits. MySQL has implicit-commit rules for many DDL statements, while PostgreSQL can roll back many schema changes.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use one table to show CREATE, INSERT, and SELECT, then state that rollback behaviour must be checked for the chosen database.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: **DDL defines structure:** `CREATE`, `ALTER`, and `DROP` work with database objects.
**DML changes rows:** `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, and `DELETE` modify stored data.
**DQL reads rows:** `SELECT` is commonly placed in this learning category.
The categories describe purpose; they do not create one universal commit rule.
Check the chosen database before assuming that a DDL statement can or cannot be rolled back.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
DDL, DML, and DQL group SQL statements by the job they perform. **DDL**, or Data Definition Language, defines database objects. `CREATE TABLE`, `ALTER TABLE`, and `DROP TABLE` change the schema. **DML**, or Data Manipulation Language, changes the rows stored inside those objects. Its common commands are `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, and `DELETE`. **DQL**, or Data Query Language, is the common teaching name for reading rows with `SELECT`.

For example, `CREATE TABLE products (...)` is DDL because it creates structure. `INSERT INTO products ...` is DML because it adds a row. `SELECT * FROM products` is DQL because it reads those rows. DCL is often used for permission commands such as `GRANT` and `REVOKE`, while TCL covers transaction commands such as `COMMIT` and `ROLLBACK`.

One important boundary is transaction behaviour. The DDL, DML, and DQL labels describe purpose, not one universal commit rule. MySQL implicitly commits around many DDL statements, but PostgreSQL allows many schema changes inside a transaction and can roll them back. So I would never say “DDL always auto-commits” without naming the database.

sections.title: SQL Command Families and Transaction Boundaries
sections.content:
**Command families describe intent**

DDL changes definitions in the database catalog: tables, columns, indexes, and other objects. DML changes the rows held by those objects. DQL reads a result set. The names make a long SQL script easier to discuss, but vendors and textbooks do not always classify every command in exactly the same way. For example, `TRUNCATE` may be grouped with DDL even though its visible result is removing rows.

**One products table**

`CREATE TABLE products (...)` creates the structure. `INSERT INTO products ...` stores a product. `SELECT id, name FROM products` reads it. The three statements work on the same data, but each has a different purpose.

**Transaction behaviour belongs to the database**

Do not infer commit behaviour only from the family name. MySQL documents implicit commits for many DDL statements. PostgreSQL supports transactional handling for many schema changes, so a `CREATE TABLE` can be undone with `ROLLBACK` in ordinary cases. Some operations and database products have different limits. Always check the documentation for the database and command you are using.

sections.title: SQL Command Families
sections.content:
blue|DDL|~defines objects|CREATE ALTER DROP|schema and catalog|commit rules vary by database
emerald|DML|~changes rows|INSERT UPDATE DELETE|normally used inside transactions|affects stored data
amber|DQL|~reads rows|SELECT|returns a result set|common teaching category
rose|DCL / TCL|~permissions + transactions|GRANT REVOKE|COMMIT ROLLBACK|related command families

sections.title: One statement from each family
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Saying DDL always auto-commits:** that is true for many statements in some databases, not a universal SQL rule.
- **Calling every SQL statement DML:** schema changes and reads have different jobs.
- **Assuming every source uses exactly the same categories:** DQL is common teaching vocabulary, while some documentation discusses `SELECT` within a broader SQL data language.
- **Ignoring the database version:** transaction support can differ by product and by command.

questions.question: What are the main DDL commands and what does each do?
questions.title: DDL Commands in SQL — CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE
questions.direct_answer: DDL changes database objects: CREATE makes an object, ALTER changes its definition, DROP removes it, and TRUNCATE quickly removes all rows while keeping the table definition. Transaction behavior is database-specific. PostgreSQL can run these operations transactionally in many cases; SQL Server supports many transactional DDL operations; MySQL normally performs implicit commits around DDL such as TRUNCATE.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the four core DDL commands and what each does.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing TRUNCATE (DDL, empties table) with DELETE (DML, removes rows).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note ALTER variants (ADD/DROP/MODIFY COLUMN) and that DDL auto-commits.

sections.title: Main DDL Commands
sections.content:
DDL can take locks and may rewrite a large table even when the syntax looks small. Adding a nullable column with no default can be cheap on one version, while changing a type can scan or rewrite every row.

Plan production DDL with database-specific documentation, backups, lock/timeout settings, and tested migrations. The statement category tells what it changes; it does not prove transactional or operational behavior.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: CREATE defines a table, index, schema, or another supported object.
ALTER changes an existing object; supported changes and locks vary.
DROP removes the object and its data/dependencies subject to database rules.
TRUNCATE removes all rows without a WHERE clause; rollback, identity reset, triggers, and foreign-key restrictions vary.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: CREATE TABLE and ALTER TABLE clearly belong to schema work. TRUNCATE is commonly grouped with DDL even though its visible result is removing data. Do not attach one auto-commit rule to the category. In PostgreSQL, a CREATE TABLE or TRUNCATE inside a transaction can be rolled back. In MySQL, TRUNCATE causes an implicit commit. Migration tooling must follow the target database's documented behavior.

sections.title: DDL Commands at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|CREATE|~make new object|table/index/view|defines structure|
emerald|ALTER|~modify object|ADD/DROP/MODIFY column|add constraints|evolves schema
rose|DROP|~delete object|structure + data gone|irreversible-ish|
amber|TRUNCATE|~empty table fast|keeps structure|resets identity|auto-commits

sections.title: CREATE, ALTER, TRUNCATE, DROP
sections.content:
```sql
CREATE TABLE customers (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(80));

ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN email VARCHAR(120);   -- add a column
ALTER TABLE customers MODIFY COLUMN name VARCHAR(120); -- change a type

TRUNCATE TABLE customers;  -- remove all rows, keep the table
DROP TABLE customers;      -- remove the table entirely
```

*`CREATE`/`ALTER` shape the schema; `TRUNCATE` empties; `DROP` removes the object.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **TRUNCATE vs DELETE**: TRUNCATE is DDL and empties the whole table; DELETE is DML and can filter rows.
- **Expecting rollback**: DDL auto-commits — a wrong DROP usually needs a restore.
- **ALTER on huge tables**: some ALTERs rewrite/lock the table — plan for it in production.
- **DROP vs TRUNCATE confusion**: DROP removes the table; TRUNCATE keeps an empty one.

beats.text: DDL stands for Data Definition Language. It's the set of commands that shape your database structure. The big four are CREATE and ALTER, DROP and TRUNCATE.
Apps change over time, so the schema changes too. DDL gives you one clean way to create new tables and reshape old ones. Without it, you'd have no way to define what your data looks like.

items: CREATE makes a new object, like a table, an index, or a view.
ALTER changes an object. It can add a column, drop one, or modify a type.
DROP deletes the whole object, structure and data together.
TRUNCATE empties a table fast but keeps the structure, and it resets the counter.

beats.text: Say you run TRUNCATE on a users table. Every row vanishes in one shot, much faster than DELETE. Here's the non-obvious part. TRUNCATE also auto-commits, so there's no rolling it back.

items: Expecting an undo. DDL auto-commits, so a wrong DROP usually means a restore.
Mixing up TRUNCATE and DELETE. TRUNCATE can't filter rows with a WHERE.

speakable_v2.cap: So those four commands define your schema. And they all commit on the spot, no rollback.

questions.question: What are DML commands in SQL and how are they used?
questions.title: DML Commands in SQL — INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE
questions.direct_answer: INSERT adds rows, UPDATE changes matching rows, and DELETE removes matching rows. These are commonly called DML. They participate in transactions according to the database, storage engine, and connection settings. UPDATE or DELETE without WHERE intentionally affects all rows, so the correct rule is to verify scope—not to claim WHERE is always required.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the DML commands and that they're transactional.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Running UPDATE/DELETE without WHERE and changing every row.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention wrapping multi-statement DML in a transaction for atomicity.

sections.title: DML Changes Table Rows
sections.content:
DML classification does not guarantee that every table/storage engine supports rollback in the same way. Most production relational tables do, but database-specific commands and nontransactional engines can differ.

Large updates can hold locks and generate substantial logs. Batch or stage them based on the engine's operational behavior, while preserving atomicity requirements. Always back up or test destructive production changes.

**Example.** INSERT INTO task(id, status) VALUES (1, 'OPEN') adds a row; UPDATE task SET status='DONE' WHERE id=1 changes it; DELETE FROM task WHERE id=1 removes it. Omitting the WHERE from UPDATE or DELETE can affect every row.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: INSERT can add one row or a set produced by another query.
UPDATE and DELETE apply to every row satisfying WHERE; without WHERE, every target row qualifies.
Use a transaction when several changes form one atomic unit.
Check row counts, locks, logging, and batching for large changes.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
UPDATE employee SET active = false intentionally changes all employees in a shutdown scenario; adding an arbitrary WHERE would be wrong. For a single employee, UPDATE employee SET active=false WHERE id=? is the intended narrow scope. Review or preview the predicate, use parameters, and check the affected row count. Auto-commit may commit each statement separately unless a transaction is started.

For example, INSERT adds a new task, UPDATE ... WHERE id=1 changes that task, and DELETE ... WHERE id=1 removes it. These data changes normally participate in a transaction, subject to the database and connection settings.

sections.title: DML at a Glance
sections.content:
emerald|INSERT|~add rows|INSERT INTO ... VALUES|or INSERT ... SELECT|new data
blue|UPDATE|~modify rows|SET col = value|needs WHERE!|changes existing data
rose|DELETE|~remove rows|with WHERE|else wipes table|removes data
amber|Transactional|~atomic changes|BEGIN ... COMMIT|or ROLLBACK|all-or-nothing

sections.title: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE in a transaction
sections.content:
```sql
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO accounts (id, balance) VALUES (1, 1000);
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1;  -- WHERE!
DELETE FROM accounts WHERE balance < 0;                    -- WHERE!
COMMIT;   -- all three changes become permanent together
```

*Wrapping the statements makes them atomic — ROLLBACK would undo all three.*

sections.title: DELETE without WHERE — wipes every row
sections.content:
```sql
-- DANGER: no WHERE clause
DELETE FROM users;
-- Removes EVERY row in users, not just the one you meant.
-- UPDATE users SET status = 'inactive';  -- same trap: sets every row
```

*The query runs fine and reports thousands of rows affected — that's the moment a fresher realizes the WHERE was missing.*

sections.title: Scoped DELETE inside a transaction — safe and reversible
sections.content:
```sql
BEGIN;
DELETE FROM users WHERE id = 42;   -- targets ONE row
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users WHERE id = 42;  -- verify before committing
COMMIT;   -- or ROLLBACK if the count looks wrong
```

*Add the WHERE first, run inside a transaction, and check the result before COMMIT — a wrong DELETE can still be rolled back.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **UPDATE/DELETE without WHERE**: changes or deletes every row — a classic disaster.
- **Forgetting to COMMIT**: changes aren't durable until committed (auto-commit varies by client).
- **Partial multi-step changes**: not using a transaction can leave data half-updated.
- **Mass updates without batching**: huge UPDATE/DELETE can lock rows and bloat logs.

speakable_v2.hook: DML changes your data. And the two scariest words in SQL? UPDATE or DELETE with no WHERE.

beats.text: DML stands for Data Manipulation Language. It's how you change the data sitting inside your tables. There are three commands. INSERT adds rows, UPDATE edits them, and DELETE removes them.
Data isn't static. Customers sign up, prices change, old records get cleared. DML gives you the verbs for all of that. Without it you could read data but never change a thing.

UPDATE changes values in rows that already exist.
DELETE removes rows, and a WHERE clause keeps it targeted.
All three are transactional, so they commit or roll back together.

beats.text: Picture a bank transfer. You subtract from one account and add to another, wrapped in one transaction. Here's the non-obvious part. If the update fails, a rollback undoes the debit, so money never goes missing.

items: Running UPDATE or DELETE with no WHERE. That hits every single row.
Forgetting to commit, so your changes never actually stick.

speakable_v2.cap: So those three commands change your data, and they're transactional. Always scope an UPDATE or DELETE with a WHERE.

questions.question: What is TCL in SQL and why is it important?
questions.title: TCL in SQL — COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT
questions.direct_answer: Transaction-control statements manage a database transaction. COMMIT makes the transaction's changes durable and visible according to isolation rules; ROLLBACK abandons uncommitted work; SAVEPOINT marks a point for partial rollback. They help implement atomicity, but the database engine provides ACID behavior. DDL interaction is database-specific—PostgreSQL can roll back many DDL statements, while MySQL implicitly commits around many of them.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know TCL commands and that they control DML transactions (ACID atomicity).
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting that DDL auto-commits, so TCL can't undo a DROP/CREATE.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Tie TCL to ACID and explain SAVEPOINT for partial rollback.

sections.title: COMMIT, ROLLBACK, and SAVEPOINT
sections.content:
Auto-commit means each successful statement is normally committed separately. Framework transaction managers change that boundary around a service operation. Isolation and locking decide what other transactions can see while work is in progress.

DDL must be checked per product and statement. PostgreSQL supports transactional CREATE/ALTER/DROP in many ordinary cases; MySQL documents implicit-commit statements. Migration tools use these facts when deciding whether a migration can be wrapped in one transaction.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Disable or leave auto-commit according to the unit-of-work boundary.
ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT undoes later work without necessarily ending the transaction.
A COMMIT can fail; applications must handle errors and uncertain external side effects.
Do not repeat the false universal rule that DDL cannot be rolled back.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: A money transfer wraps the debit and credit in one transaction, commits only after both succeed, and rolls back on failure. A savepoint can recover one optional step while preserving earlier work when the business rule permits it. This mechanism covers database changes in that transaction; it does not automatically undo an email or remote HTTP call already sent.

sections.title: TCL at a Glance
sections.content:
emerald|COMMIT|~make permanent|ends transaction|changes durable|
rose|ROLLBACK|~undo changes|back to start|or to a SAVEPOINT|
blue|SAVEPOINT|~partial marker|roll back part|keep earlier work|nested control
amber|Why|~ACID atomicity|all-or-nothing|protects multi-step DML|DDL auto-commits anyway

sections.title: COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Expecting to ROLLBACK DDL**: DDL auto-commits — you can't undo a DROP/ALTER with ROLLBACK.
- **Forgetting to COMMIT**: work stays uncommitted (and may be lost on disconnect).
- **Long-running transactions**: holding locks too long blocks other users.
- **Misusing SAVEPOINT**: it's for partial undo within one transaction, not a substitute for COMMIT.

seo.metaTitle: TCL in SQL — COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT — java backend interview question | InterviewExplainer
seo.metaDescription: Interview answer for What is TCL in SQL and why is it important? with a clear explanation, practical example, common mistakes, and follow-up questions.

speakable_v2.hook: TCL's the safety net under your data. COMMIT keeps your changes, ROLLBACK erases them, and SAVEPOINT undoes just a piece.
speakable_v2.standard_example: a payment insert with a SAVEPOINT before the balance update

beats.text: TCL stands for Transaction Control Language. It's how you control a transaction around your DML changes. The three commands are COMMIT, ROLLBACK, and SAVEPOINT.
Some jobs need several changes to land together, or not at all. A money transfer is the classic case. TCL lets you commit the whole group, or roll it back if one step breaks.

items: COMMIT makes every change in the transaction permanent.
ROLLBACK throws those changes away and goes back to the start.
SAVEPOINT drops a named marker for rolling back to later.
Together they give DML the all-or-nothing behavior we call atomicity.

beats.text: Say you insert a payment, then update a balance. You set a SAVEPOINT after the insert. Here's the non-obvious part. If the balance update looks wrong, you roll back to that savepoint and keep the payment.

items: Trying to roll back DDL. It auto-commits, so TCL can't touch it.
Holding a transaction open too long, which blocks other users.

speakable_v2.cap: So COMMIT saves, ROLLBACK undoes, and SAVEPOINT marks a partial restore point. But none of it works on DDL.

questions.question: Why do DDL statements auto-commit in most databases?
questions.title: Why DDL Statements Auto-Commit in SQL
questions.direct_answer: The premise that DDL always or necessarily auto-commits is false. Some databases make many DDL statements transactional, while others issue implicit commits for some or most DDL. PostgreSQL can roll back common DDL in a transaction; MySQL performs implicit commits around many DDL statements, including TRUNCATE. Schema changes can therefore sit inside a transaction on supported systems.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand why DDL auto-commits and its impact on open transactions.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming a DDL inside a transaction can be rolled back with the DML around it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note this is engine-dependent (some DBs support transactional DDL) and that DDL commits pending DML.

sections.title: DDL Transaction Behavior Depends on the Database
sections.content:
Why vendors differ is implementation design: catalogs, locks, storage engines, and recovery systems expose different capabilities. It is not a law of SQL. Even in a database with transactional DDL, some commands cannot run inside a transaction block or have non-transactional effects.

Migration tools may wrap migrations in transactions only when supported. Verify the exact statement and server version before relying on rollback, and never mix unrelated data changes with DDL on a system that can implicitly commit them.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: DDL means schema/object definition, not one transaction rule.
PostgreSQL supports transactional behavior for many ordinary DDL statements.
MySQL documents statements that cause implicit commits.
Locks, online-DDL options, sequence/database creation, and other exceptions remain vendor-specific.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: If PostgreSQL runs BEGIN; CREATE TABLE demo(...); ROLLBACK;, the table can disappear with the rollback. That directly disproves 'schema cannot sit half-applied'. In MySQL, CREATE TABLE or TRUNCATE normally commits an active transaction according to its implicit-commit rules. Oracle also commonly performs implicit commits around DDL. The correct interview answer names the database before describing the behavior.

sections.title: DDL Auto-Commit at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|What happens|~implicit COMMIT|commits pending DML first|then runs DDL|then commits DDL
rose|Consequence|~no rollback|CREATE/ALTER/DROP permanent|ends your transaction|backup before risky DDL
amber|Why|~schema not row-level|hard to reverse cleanly|other sessions need consistency|
emerald|Engine note|~not universal|MySQL/Oracle auto-commit|PostgreSQL transactional DDL|verify your DB

sections.title: DDL commits the DML around it
sections.content:
```sql
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO logs VALUES (1, 'start');   -- pending DML

CREATE TABLE temp_report (id INT);       -- DDL: implicit COMMIT here!
-- the INSERT above is now COMMITTED and can no longer be rolled back

ROLLBACK;   -- too late for the INSERT; only affects work AFTER the DDL
```

*In MySQL/Oracle the DDL silently commits the earlier INSERT — a common surprise.*

sections.title: Expecting ROLLBACK to undo a DDL (MySQL)
sections.content:
```sql
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO orders (id, total) VALUES (1, 50);
DROP TABLE old_orders;   -- DDL: implicit COMMIT — the INSERT is now permanent
ROLLBACK;                -- does NOT bring old_orders back, and the INSERT stays
```

*A fresher assumes the whole block is one transaction. In MySQL the DROP already committed everything before it.*

sections.title: Keep DDL out of the DML transaction
sections.content:
```sql
-- Finish (or roll back) the data transaction FIRST
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO orders (id, total) VALUES (1, 50);
COMMIT;   -- or ROLLBACK — decided cleanly, on its own

-- Then run schema changes separately, with a backup ready
DROP TABLE old_orders;   -- auto-commits, as expected
```

*Separate the two: settle DML in its own transaction, then run DDL on its own — no surprise commits.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Expecting rollback of DDL**: a wrong DROP/ALTER usually needs a restore.
- **Mixing DDL into a DML transaction**: the DDL commits your pending DML unexpectedly.
- **Assuming all engines behave alike**: PostgreSQL supports transactional DDL; MySQL/Oracle don't.
- **No backup before risky schema changes**: there's no ROLLBACK to save you.

seo.metaTitle: Why DDL Statements Auto-Commit in SQL — java backend interview question | InterviewExplainer
seo.metaDescription: Interview answer for Why do DDL statements auto-commit in most databases? with a clear explanation, practical example, common mistakes, and follow-up questions.

speakable_v2.hook: Run a CREATE mid-transaction in MySQL and it quietly commits your earlier inserts too. That's DDL's hidden auto-commit.
speakable_v2.standard_example: an INSERT followed by CREATE TABLE in one MySQL session

beats.text: DDL auto-commits because it changes the database structure itself, not just the rows. A schema change can't really sit half-done inside a transaction. So most engines make it permanent the moment it runs.
Schema changes are hard to undo cleanly at the row level. And other sessions need a steady view of the tables. So the engine commits right away instead of keeping the change pending.

items: First it commits any DML you already had open.
Then it runs the DDL and commits that too.
Then it starts a fresh transaction for the work that follows.
So a single CREATE or DROP lands instantly, with no undo.

beats.text: Say you INSERT a few rows, then run a CREATE TABLE in the same session. Here's the non-obvious part. That CREATE quietly commits your inserts too, so a later rollback can't reach them.

items: Assuming a DROP will undo. In MySQL it really won't.
Mixing DDL into open DML work, which commits it by surprise.

speakable_v2.cap: So DDL commits the moment it runs, and it drags your pending DML along. PostgreSQL's the rare exception.
